sections.h2: What makes a University City, MO sale different from other St. Louis County suburbs?
sections.html:
University City is an inner-ring suburb of St. Louis in St. Louis County, and its housing stock is older than most of the county around it. The city has a rule that matters to every seller: a house sold or rented here needs a city occupancy permit before anyone moves in, and the city suggests arranging the inspection before you list. Plan around that step early, because it shapes repairs, timing and what a buyer, whether a family or an investor, has to do after closing.

The 2020 census found 35,065 residents. The July 2025 estimate is 34,657, a dip of 1.6 percent. Streetcar-era blocks in the south and postwar blocks in the north sit within a few miles of each other, so condition and layout vary from one street to the next.

sections.h2: How old is University City, and does that matter to a seller?
sections.html:
University City is a streetcar suburb. According to Wikipedia, the older southern portion keeps much of its historic architecture, especially around Delmar Boulevard, while the northern part developed mostly after World War II and has more shopping centers and car-oriented development. A buyer looking at a 1920s house south of Delmar is comparing different things than a buyer looking at a postwar house north of Olive.

The city was incorporated in September 1906 after publisher Edward Gardner Lewis bought 85 acres northwest of Forest Park and built a model town. His octagonal Magazine Building, a 135-foot tower, is now City Hall at 6801 Delmar Boulevard. Between 1910 and 1920 the city grew faster than any other in Missouri, and the biggest wave of housing construction came after World War II.

The city covers 5.9 square miles and is bounded roughly by Skinker Boulevard on the east and Interstate 170 on the west. Heman Park, at 85 acres, and the Ruth Park golf course are the largest green spaces. Midland Boulevard runs along the divide between the Mississippi and Missouri River watersheds, and the River Des Peres rises near the University City and Clayton line.

sections.h2: Must a University City house pass an inspection before it sells?
sections.html:
Yes, plan on one. The city says anyone moving into University City must apply for and receive an occupancy permit before moving in, and that anyone planning to sell should arrange an inspection before the house goes on the market. The inspection fee for a home sale is $80 per unit.

  • File with Planning and Zoning on the fourth floor of City Hall, 6801 Delmar Boulevard, or email inspections@ucitymo.org.
  • The application fee is $25 and is not refundable. Card payments carry a 3.25 percent convenience fee.
  • Inspectors check electrical, plumbing, heating and general building condition against the property maintenance code.
  • A valid driver's license, state ID or passport is accepted as identification.

If the house fails, the city requires corrections. For minor repairs it may issue a conditional occupancy permit for $35, which gives the owner 60 days to finish the work while people live there. Miss that 60-day mark and the city may notify owner and residents that occupancy is no longer valid, and legal action can follow.

sections.h2: Which sale routes fit a University City house?
sections.html:
Three routes exist: an agent listing, a sale you run yourself, or an offer from an investor who buys houses in their current state. Each route runs into the same occupancy requirement, so ask each buyer who will order the inspection and who pays for repairs.

  • List on the market. You pay the inspection fee, fix what the inspector flags, and ask your agent for the commission rate and the likely closing timeline.
  • Sell it yourself. You save an agent's fee but handle pricing, showings, the contract and the city paperwork.
  • Sell to an investor. A buyer paying cash is not waiting on a lender. Weigh each offer against what a listing would leave you after repairs, the inspection and closing costs.

Houses with a failed inspection, a holdover tenant or an estate still in probate are harder to list. Those are the situations where investor offers tend to come up. Get at least two written offers and read what each says about who pays closing costs.

sections.h2: Who bills University City property tax, and what are the dates?
sections.html:
St. Louis County, not the city, bills the tax: the Assessor sets the value and the Collector of Revenue collects. The bill for a year is on time if paid or postmarked by December 31. The Collector's FAQ describes interest of up to 18 percent a year plus a 2 percent penalty after that, citing RSMo chapters 139 and 140.

State law has the Assessor revalue every parcel in odd-numbered years, which makes 2027 the next one. Appeals go to the independent Board of Equalization from May 1 through the second Monday in July. The July 13, 2026 cutoff is behind us, and filing reopens May 1, 2027. The Collector's office is at 41 S. Central Avenue in Clayton and answers at (314) 615-7100. If your account is behind, the back tax team at (314) 615-7865 can give the payoff and explain redemption limits.

Two relief programs are worth a question: the county's Senior Property Tax Freeze and the state's Property Tax Credit, nicknamed the Circuit Breaker. If anything is owed, have the title company show the balance on the settlement statement so it is paid out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: What else should a University City seller check?
sections.html:
The School District of University City runs the public schools, including University City High School, and is managed separately from other districts in the area. Name it in your listing, since families often search by district.

Find out from your title company which county office records the deed. After closing, shut off your utilities and hand over the keys with any permit paperwork. A current tenant changes the picture, so check the occupancy permit status before the buyer closes.

  • Gather the last occupancy permit, any repair receipts and warranties.
  • Look for open permits on old additions or finished basements.
  • Ask the title company about unpaid city or county charges.

faqs.q: Is an inspection needed to sell in University City?
faqs.a: The city asks sellers to schedule one before listing, and whoever moves in must hold an occupancy permit. A sale inspection runs $80 per unit, on top of the $25 application fee.

faqs.q: What happens if my University City house fails the occupancy inspection?
faqs.a: Corrections are required. A conditional permit at $35 can cover minor items and allows 60 days to finish them, after which an unfinished job can cost the permit.

faqs.q: What is the tax due date for a house in University City?
faqs.a: December 31 of the billing year. Later postmarks add interest and a penalty, so a 2026 balance should be settled through the title company at closing.

faqs.q: Is the 2026 assessment appeal window for University City still open?
faqs.a: No, July 13 was the cutoff. Next year's filing period starts May 1, 2027, in the county's reassessment year.

faqs.q: Do owners or renters dominate University City?
faqs.a: Owners hold 56.2 percent of homes per the Census Bureau, so landlords are a large share of buyers. Owners put the median value at $306,700.
